title: Man. Post. Cap. II §XIX: Garissoles — Alio colore / three modes; habitus imputation charge
pass_a_gloss: GAR. Then with another color they paint this later imputation of theirs, when they add that nothing stands in the way why Adam's sin should not be said to be imputed to us, inasmuch as our hereditary vice is a habit which the first actual sin left in Adam's soul; then an inclination to similar sins; third a habitual consent to that sin. These words the Learned Man drew from the second letter which I had written to him: but of his own he added the words inasmuch as, then, third, dividing what I had joined, and from one reason making three against my mind. I will copy out entire the place from that letter written in French. Adam's sin can be said to be imputed to us his posterity in three ways. First, because (as Calvin hints, calling the vice which flowed from Adam into us Adam's sin) it is within us. Second, because when hereditary vice makes us equally worthy of eternal death as Adam, nothing stands in the way why Adam's sin should not be said to be imputed to us in that sense in which the Apostle said, if anyone has kept the law, his foreskin is imputed for circumcision, that is, that he is held in the same place as if he had been circumcised. Third, because hereditary corruption is a habit which the first sin left in Adam's soul, and a perverse inclination to a like sin; and therefore a habitual consent to that sin, I see nothing that prevents it from being said to be imputed to us. This last mode, this last reason, the Learned Man has torn into three, and changes it because of inasmuch as. But let us hear him. GAR. Where first that comes to be wondered at, that they acknowledge Adam's sin to be imputed, inasmuch as our corruption is a habit left in Adam's soul. For these words seem to prefer the imputation of Adam's habitual sin itself. But what is more horrible or absurd, in that we say Adam's actual sin is imputed to us, than that by these words they confess habitual sin is imputed? especially since imputation seems rather to be referred to acts than to habits?
pass_b_english: Garissoles: They next dress this later imputation in fresh paint: nothing, they say, blocks calling Adam's sin imputed to us inasmuch as our hereditary vice is a habit the first actual sin left in Adam's soul; next, an inclination toward like sins; third, habitual consent to that sin. He lifted those words from my second letter to him—then slipped in of his own 'inasmuch as,' 'next,' and 'third,' carving one joined reason into three against my sense. Here is the whole French-letter place. Adam's sin may be said imputed to us his posterity three ways. First: as Calvin hints (naming Adam's sin the vice that flowed from him into us), it is inside us. Second: hereditary vice makes us as worthy of eternal death as Adam, so nothing stops saying Adam's sin is imputed in the Apostle's sense—if someone has kept the law, his foreskin is imputed for circumcision (Romans 2:26), i.e. he is counted as circumcised. Third: hereditary corruption is the habit the first sin left in Adam's soul, plus a bent toward a like sin, and so habitual consent to that sin—I see no bar to saying it is imputed to us. That last mode, that last reason, the learned man has shredded into three and warped with 'inasmuch as.' Hear him. Garissoles: First wonder: they grant Adam's sin imputed inasmuch as our corruption is a habit left in Adam's soul. The wording seems to favor imputing Adam's habitual sin itself. What could be worse—when we speak of imputing Adam's actual sin—than confessing by these words that a habitual sin is imputed? Especially when imputation looks to acts, not habits.
source_text: GAR. Alio deinde colore hanc posteriorem suam imputationem pingunt, cum addunt, nihil obstare, quominus Adami peccatum nobis imputari dicatur, quatenus vitium nostrum haereditarium habitus est, quem primum actuale peccatum reliquit in Adami anima; deinde inclinatio ad similia peccata; tertio consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum. Haec verba ex secunda, quam ad eum scripseram, epistola Vir Doctus deprompsit: sed de suo addidit voces quatenus, deinde, tertio, dividens ea quae conjunxi, ac ex una ratione tres conficiens praeter mentem meam. Locum ex illa epistola Gallice scripta integrum exscribam. Peccatum Adami dici potest nobis ejus posteris imputari tribus modis. Primo, quia (ut innuit Calvinus, vitium quod ab Adamo in nos defluxit peccatum Adami vocans) intra nos est. Secundo, quia cum vitium haereditarium nos aeque morte aeterna dignos ac Adamum faciat, nihil obstat, quominus peccatum Adami nobis eo sensu dicatur imputari, quo dixit Apostolus, si quis legem servaverit, illius praeputium in circuncisionem imputari, hoc est, eodem loco eum haberi ac si fuisset circumcissus. Tertio, quia corruptio haereditaria est habitus, quem primum peccatum in Adami anima reliquit, & perversa inclinatio ad simile peccatum; ac proinde consensus habitualis ad illud peccatum, nihil video quod impediat, quominus nobis imputari dicatur. Hunc ultimum modum, hanc ultimam rationem, Vir Doctus in tres discerpsit, ac mutat quia in quatenus. Sed eum audiamus. GAR. Ubi primum illud mirari subit, quod imputari agnoscunt peccatum Adae, quatenus corruptio nostra est habitus in Adami anima relictus. Haec enim verba praeferre videntur imputationem ipsius habitualis peccati Adae. Quid autem horridius aut absurdius est, in eo quod dicimus, imputari nobis peccatum Adami actuale, quam quod his verbis fatentur, imputari peccatum habituate? praesertim cum imputatio potius ad actus videatur referenda quam ad habitus?

choices.choice: Keep French-letter three modes and quatenus split charge
